question: Regulation (EU) No 1129/20111 has been in force since 2011. This regulation prohibits the treatment of citrus fruits with certain additives (E230, E231 and E232), while the fungicide and pesticide thiabendazole (E233) and imazalil – which is sprayed onto the surface of citrus fruits to prolong their storage – are still permitted.

Several studies, including some carried out by the US Environmental Protection Agency, have found this latter substance to be carcinogenic. If peel has been treated with fungicides, additives or preservatives, this must be indicated on the label. By law, producers must indicate on their labels any treatments carried out with waxes and other substances.

Where imazalil is among the additives used, the law requires a mandatory warning – ‘inedible peel’ – to be provided on the label. These requirements, however, do not apply to pomelos, grapefruits and limes. Can the Commission clarify the following points: 1.
What level of enforcement is in place to ensure that the prescribed maximum residue limits (MRLs) are adhered to?
When were the MRLs last reviewed and have they taken into account the latest scientific data?
Why is the mandatory warning on the use of the peel (inedible peel) not extended to limes?

Commission Regulation (EU) No 1129/2011 of 11 November 2011 amending Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council by establishing a Union list of food additives (OJ L 295, 12.11.2011, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/1129/oj).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 on maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides1 imposes Member States to carry out controls to ensure that food placed on the market is compliant with the legal limits.

The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) collects the information from national and EU-coordinated control programmes and publishes the EU report on pesticide residues in food2. In 2024, 86 449 samples were analysed. 96% contained no residues or residues below or equal to the MRLs. Non-compliant samples (1.8%) triggered sanctions or enforcement actions.

Out of 38 169 samples analysed for the presence of imazalil, including fruits with their peel3, only 35 contained residues above the MRL. This confirms that the food available to EU consumers is safe. The MRLs for imazalil were last updated in 20204 considering EFSA’s opinion of 20195. Although imazalil is classified as carcinogen category 2, recent studies reviewed by EFSA6, show that it is not genotoxic.

Further EFSA opinions confirmed that new MRLs for imazalil do not present a risk for consumers4,7. The Commission prepared new draft Regulations reviewing some MRLs for imazalil that are under discussion with Member States. The food additives authorised for surface treatment of citrus and/or other fruits, and their conditions of use, are laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1333/20088.

Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/24299 lays down the marketing standard for citrus fruit, which lists the ‘commercial specifications’ required to appear on each package10. This includes: ‘When used, mention of the preserving agent or other chemical substances used at post-harvest stage’. This requirement applies to all citrus species covered by the marketing standard, which includes limes, pummelos and grapefruits11.
1 ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2005/396/oj. 2 EFSA (2026). The 2024 European Union report on pesticide residues in food. EFSA Journal, 24, e10054.
